query: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloys are promising bond-coat candidates because of their mechanical properties and elevated-temperature oxidation resistance. Earlier HVAF-M3 work identified 15–45 μm feedstock as optimal for high-quality coatings, but applying the same composition and size range with the HVAF-i7 torch yielded acceptable coating quality yet inadequate thickness. Separate studies of conventional MCrAlY bond coats using the M3 system reported a slight gain in deposition efficiency at higher particle velocity and nozzle-specific best spray distances of 300 and 350 mm. The design target is a sufficiently thick, adherent bond coat that retains coating integrity, minimal as-sprayed oxidation, and durability during high-temperature thermal-barrier service, including deposition within internal diameters as small as 120 mm. What single intervention could overcome the thickness limitation? State the hypothesized intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, define the deposition and service conditions under which it should remain effective, identify supporting evidence from the cited prior studies, and propose a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adjusting the spray distance during HVAF-i7 deposition to 300–350 mm will increase the particle velocity upon impact, resulting in improved deposition efficiency and thicker FeCoNiCrAl bond coats.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy feedstock with a particle size range of 15–45 μm
generation.intervention: Modify the HVAF-i7 spray process by setting the nozzle-to-substrate distance to 300–350 mm instead of the current shorter distance.
generation.conditions: HVAF-i7 deposition on substrates (including internal diameters as small as 120 mm) under conditions similar to previous tests, ensuring comparable thermal and oxidation environments during high-temperature thermal-barrier service.
generation.structural_mediator: Higher in-flight particle kinetic energy leads to better splat formation and lower rebound, thereby increasing the material build-up per pass.
generation.mechanism: By increasing the spray distance, the particles gain additional acceleration time in the combustion jet, resulting in a higher velocity upon impact. This enhanced kinetic energy improves the bonding efficiency and reduces particle scattering, thereby producing a thicker, adherent deposit while maintaining low in-spray oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified spray distance will yield a significantly thicker bond coat compared to the baseline (15–45 μm feedstock at the standard distance) while preserving coating quality, adherence, and minimal oxidation.
generation.baseline: Coatings deposited using 15–45 μm feedstock with the HVAF-i7 torch at the original spray distance yielding acceptable quality but inadequate thickness.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to remain effective for both standard and confined geometries (internal diameters down to 120 mm) and under the thermal and oxidative conditions typical of high-temperature thermal-barrier applications.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative increase in thickness and any secondary effects on oxidation levels or microstructural integrity remain uncertain until experimentally verified. Additionally, the adaptation to the HVAF-i7 system’s operational limits in confined geometries warrants further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a controlled experiment comparing coatings deposited at the current spray distance versus 300–350 mm using the same 15–45 μm feedstock and HVAF-i7 torch. All other deposition parameters (fuel type, feed rate, substrate preparation, etc.) should be kept constant. Measure and compare the coating thickness, adhesion strength, porosity, and oxide content.
measurements: Adhesion strength (quantified via standardized pull-off tests)
Porosity (analyzed using image analysis of cross-sections)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If coatings deposited at 300–350 mm do not show a statistically significant increase in thickness while maintaining or improving adhesion and oxidation properties compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 4 shows the difference in the properties based on the spraying distance. As the spraying distance increases, the average thickness of the coatings slightly decreases due to a stronger scattering of the particles on the longer path. An increase in the spraying distance results in an increase in coating porosity. Porosity depends on the temperature and kinetic energy of the particles []. Particles sprayed from a longer distance have a lower kinetic energy when they strike the substrate, which results in increased porosity. High temperatures and exposure to oxygen lead to the in-flight oxidation of particles; the smaller particles undergo more severe oxidation. With an increase in the spraying distance, the particles are exposed to oxygen for a longer time, which leads to an increased content of oxides (Figure 4d). As the particles oxidize with the formation of alumina, BCC solid solution loses aluminum, which is reflected in a decrease in its lattice parameter (Figure 3b). It is known [] that when Al concentration in FeCoNiCrAlMo0.5 is lower than 10%, FCC solid solution becomes preferable to BCC.
